subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A 'foil' is a character who...
options: Contrasts with another to highlight that character's qualities
Speaks only in soliloquies
Always dies at the end
Narrates the whole story
questions.explain: A foil's contrasting traits throw another character's qualities into sharper relief.

questions.q: The 'protagonist' of a text is...
options: The narrator only
The character who opposes the hero
Any minor character
The central character whose journey drives the narrative
questions.explain: The protagonist is the main character at the centre of the action, often in conflict with an antagonist.

questions.q: In a poem, 'enjambment' is when a line runs on into the next without end-stop punctuation. What effect can this create?
options: A sense of momentum, flow or breathlessness that mirrors meaning
A pause in the middle of a line
A fixed, regular beat in every line
A repeated sound at the end of lines
questions.explain: Enjambment carries sense over the line break, often creating flow, urgency or a spilling-over effect that can reflect the poem's content.

questions.q: 'Iambic pentameter' is a line with...
options: Exactly four rhyming words
Ten lines of equal length
No regular pattern at all
Five pairs of unstressed-then-stressed syllables
questions.explain: Iambic pentameter contains five iambs (da-DUM x5), giving roughly ten syllables and a rhythm close to natural speech.

questions.q: Why might a writer use 'foreshadowing'?
options: To hint at events to come, building tension or a sense of inevitability
To confuse the reader about the genre
To end the text abruptly
To list the characters' names
questions.explain: Foreshadowing plants clues about later events, creating suspense or a feeling that an outcome is unavoidable.

questions.q: 'Blank verse' is...
options: A poem left unfinished
Poetry with no words
Unrhymed iambic pentameter
A stanza of exactly four lines
questions.explain: Blank verse is unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter, much used by Shakespeare for noble characters.

questions.q: 'Pathetic fallacy' is a technique in which a writer...
options: Gives weather or nature human emotions to reflect mood
Uses very simple vocabulary deliberately
Repeats a word for emphasis
Addresses an absent person directly
questions.explain: Pathetic fallacy projects human feelings onto the natural world or weather, often mirroring a character's emotional state.

questions.q: A 'symbol' in literature is best described as...
options: An object, image or action that stands for a larger idea
A pause in the middle of a line
The main character of a story
A word that rhymes with another
questions.explain: A symbol carries meaning beyond its literal self, representing an abstract idea such as hope, death or freedom.

questions.q: Which sentence best embeds a quotation effectively?
options: 'Green-eyed monster.' This is about jealousy and it is in the play.
The quote is 'green-eyed monster' which means jealousy.
Shakespeare says jealousy. Quote: 'green-eyed monster'.
Iago warns against jealousy, the 'green-eyed monster', presenting it as a predator that 'mock[s]' its victim.
questions.explain: A good embed weaves the short quotation smoothly into the writer's own sentence and begins to analyse the method.

questions.q: A recurring image or idea running through a text is called a...
options: motif
caesura
stanza
volta
questions.explain: A motif is a repeated image, object or idea that builds and reinforces a theme across the text.

questions.q: 'Dramatic irony' occurs when...
options: Two characters say the same line
The audience knows something a character does not
A character speaks in rhyme
The play ends happily
questions.explain: Dramatic irony arises from the gap between the audience's knowledge and a character's ignorance, creating tension or poignancy.

questions.q: How does a 'soliloquy' differ from an 'aside'?
options: A soliloquy is delivered alone; an aside is a brief remark while others are on stage
They are identical in every way
An aside can only be spoken by the protagonist
An aside is always longer than a soliloquy
questions.explain: An aside is a quick comment heard only by the audience while other characters remain on stage, whereas a soliloquy is spoken when the character is alone.

questions.q: A 'soliloquy' in a play is best defined as...
options: A conversation between two characters
A short comment to the audience while others are present
Stage directions printed in italics
A speech where a character alone on stage reveals their inner thoughts
questions.explain: In a soliloquy the character is alone and voices private thoughts, letting the audience access their inner mind.

questions.q: What does the assessment objective concerning 'a critical, personal response' reward?
options: Copying the question back as a statement
Your own thoughtful interpretation, supported by evidence from the text
Agreeing with a memorised essay
Avoiding any opinion at all
questions.explain: Examiners credit a considered personal interpretation that is anchored in textual evidence rather than a generic, borrowed view.

questions.q: When a writer uses an 'antagonist', this character mainly functions to...
options: Speak only in rhyming verse
Provide comic relief in every scene
Oppose the protagonist and create conflict that drives the plot
Narrate events from a neutral standpoint
questions.explain: The antagonist stands against the protagonist, generating the conflict that propels a narrative forward.

questions.q: A 'sonnet' is most reliably identified by which feature?
options: A refrain repeated after every stanza
Fourteen lines, usually in iambic pentameter, with a structured rhyme scheme
Exactly three stanzas of six lines
An absence of any punctuation
questions.explain: The fourteen-line structure with a regular rhyme scheme and a turn is the hallmark of the sonnet form.

questions.q: A 'tragedy', as a literary form, typically...
options: Charts the downfall of a central figure, often through a flaw or fate
Is always written in free verse
Contains no serious events
Ends happily with a marriage
questions.explain: A tragedy traces the protagonist's decline and downfall, frequently linked to a personal flaw or forces beyond their control.

questions.q: A 'caesura' is a deliberate pause within a line of poetry. Which is the BEST analytical comment on its effect?
options: It always signals the end of the poem
It forces a break that can fragment the rhythm and emphasise the words around it
It tells us the poet's date of birth
It guarantees the poem is a sonnet
questions.explain: A caesura interrupts the line's flow, drawing attention to surrounding words and sometimes mirroring disruption or hesitation.

questions.q: To gain marks for using context, you should...
options: List as many dates as possible
Retell the historical period in a separate paragraph
Avoid mentioning the writer altogether
Link relevant context to how it shapes meaning or the reader's response
questions.explain: Context earns credit when it illuminates the text's meaning or effect, not when it is merely recounted as history.

questions.q: Which response best matches what GCSE Assessment Objectives reward?
options: Analysing the writer's methods, their effect on the reader and the writer's intentions
Describing your personal weekend
Counting the number of words on a page
Summarising the plot in detail
questions.explain: Higher marks come from analysing methods, effects on the reader and authorial purpose rather than retelling the story.

questions.q: When using a quotation, which is the strongest analytical practice?
options: Zoom in on a single significant word and analyse its connotations
Choose the longest quotation available
Only paraphrase, never quote
Quote without any explanation
questions.explain: Selecting a precise word and exploring its connotations shows close, detailed engagement with the writer's choices.

questions.q: When tracking a theme across a whole text, the strongest approach is to...
options: Ignore structure entirely
Trace how the theme develops and changes from beginning to end
Quote only from the final page
Mention the theme once in your introduction
questions.explain: Examining how a theme is introduced, developed and resolved shows a 'whole-text' understanding that examiners reward.
